To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the use of calcium carbonate (1 g, three times daily) for a period of 7 days significantly reduces the severity and frequency of diarrhoea in NFV‐treated HIV‐infected subjects, and (2) this effect is not associated with a significant increase in NFV or M8 exposure.

the calcium carbonate (CC) supplementation significantly improved nelfinavir associated diarrhoea in the HIV‐infected subjects, and did not alter the pharmacokinetics parameters of nelfinavirus and its active metabolite M 8.

the addition of calcium carbonate to nelfinavir therapy in HIV‐inflicted patients with nelfiavir‐associated diarrheas, is associated with a significant decrease in nelfinivir‐associated diarrhea and no significant changes in the pharmacokinetics parameters of nelfinivair and M8.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis of calcium carbonate, calcium carbonate powder, calcium carbonate granules and calcium carbonate pellets, and the production of calcium carbonate.
the development of new, more efficient, and less expensive methods of calcium carbonate precipitation.

the use of calcium carbonate for the prevention of osteoporosis and osteopenia in postmenopausal women, the prevention and treatment of bone fractures in postmenopusal women, and the prevention of osteopenia and bone fractures in men.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the evidence is insufficient to recommend calcium carbonate supplementation for the management of HIV‐associated diarrhea, and that the evidence is also insufficient to recommend calcium supplementation for the prevention of HIV-associated diarrhea.
calcium carbonate has no significant effect on the pharmacokinetic profile of nelfinavirus.
the evidence is insufficient to recommend the routine use of calcium supplementation for prevention or treatment of osteoporosis in patients with HIV.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that calcium carbonate can reduce the severity of diarrhoea in patients receiving nelfinavir therapy.
calcium carbonate is effective for treating diarrhea in patients taking nelfinavir.
the calcium carbonate was effective in treating nelfinavir associated diarrhea in our study, with no significant changes to nelfinavir or M8 concentrations.
The main takeaway from our work is that
calcium carbonate is a good option for treating nelfinavir-associated diarrhoea in the HIV population.
the use of calcium supplements in patients with NFV‐associated diarrhoeae is safe and effective in reducing diarrhoeal episodes.
the use of calcium carbonate to treat nelfinavir-associated diarrhea is not recommended because it does not improve diarrhea and may increase the risk of kidney stones.
